response:
Reward model overoptimization asks: as a policy is optimized against a learned reward model, at what point does higher reward-model score correspond to lower true human preference satisfaction — and how does the choice of reference policy shape that cliff? The core tension is that any reward model is a lossy, finite-sample proxy for the true reward, so a sufficiently capable optimizer will find inputs that exploit the proxy's errors rather than genuinely satisfy the underlying preference. The "frozen reference policy" setup (standard KL-penalized RLHF, where the KL term anchors the policy to a fixed SFT checkpoint) creates a stationary exploitation target: the optimizer's search space is bounded, but the bound itself never adapts to what the policy has already learned. A co-evolving reference — where the reference policy is periodically updated to track the current policy, as in some iterated RLHF or online DPO schemes — relaxes that anchor, which can accelerate capability gain but also accelerates the policy's ability to reach and exploit low-density regions of the reward model's input space that were never covered by human raters. What an expert worries about that a beginner misses is the compounding problem in iterated rounds: each new reward model is trained on data generated by the previous policy, so distributional shift between the policy's outputs and the reward model's training support widens every round, and the KL penalty that looked safe in round one is no longer anchoring the policy to anything the reward model was calibrated on.

NEXT: If the KL penalty's protective effect depends on the reward model being well-calibrated near the reference policy's support, what happens to that calibration guarantee specifically when you update the reference policy to the current policy between rounds?

The KL penalty was doing useful work in round one because the SFT checkpoint sat inside the reward model's training distribution; after one round of optimization, the current policy already occupies higher-reward, lower-density regions of that distribution, and declaring that the new reference doesn't restore calibration, it just resets the nominal distance to zero while the actual extrapolation error persists. Gao et al. The amplification mechanism is selection pressure acting on reward model errors: the optimizer doesn't treat all reward model mistakes equally — it finds and concentrates probability mass on whichever outputs score highest, so a region where the reward model over-estimates by even a modest amount becomes the mode of the next policy, which then becomes the training distribution for the next reward model. This is importantly different from mere inheritance: if round-k's reward model has a +0.3 logit error in some narrow output region, round-k's policy will oversample that region, meaning round-(k+1)'s reward model is trained on a dataset that is disproportionately drawn from exactly the flawed region, likely fitting and then extrapolating the error rather than correcting it. The mechanism has a formal analog in boosting and active learning gone wrong: you are doing something like hard-example mining, except the "hard examples" are selected adversarially by the optimizer, not chosen to reduce generalization error. Anthropic's work on Constitutional AI and iterative RLHF implicitly acknowledges this by using a separate held-out preference model for evaluation, precisely because the training RM's scores become unreliable as a ground-truth signal once it has been round-tripped through policy optimization. Kumar et al. (2020, "Conservative Objective Models" in offline RL) analyzed the directly analogous problem in model-based RL, showing that a learned value function optimized by a policy generates OOD queries that cause the model to extrapolate overoptimistically, and that the extrapolation error grows super-linearly with optimization steps — the same geometry applies here because a reward model is a value function being optimized against. The crux is that ordinary supervised learning assumes the test distribution is the same as the training distribution; iterative RLHF systematically violates this by construction, and each round tightens the adversarial feedback loop.

The most principled approach would be importance weighting: down-weight training examples in proportion to how much the current policy over-represents them relative to some anchor distribution, which would in theory correct for the adversarial sampling bias. The catch is that computing the correct importance weights requires knowing the density ratio between the corrupted collection policy and the true preference-elicitation distribution — but that ratio is precisely what you don't have, because the "true" distribution is latent human judgment, not any observed policy. Ensemble-based uncertainty estimation offers a partial substitute: if you train a committee of reward models and down-weight or flag examples where the ensemble disagrees, you can detect regions of high extrapolation error, which correlates with (though is not identical to) the corrupted regions — Gleave & Irving (2022, "Uncertainty Estimation for Language Reward Models") explored this and found ensemble spread was a meaningful signal but systematically underestimated uncertainty in the exact high-reward tail regions where it matters most, because all ensemble members are trained on the same skewed data. A more radical fix is to interleave targeted human re-annotation specifically on the high-reward outputs the current policy favors, essentially injecting fresh on-distribution signal into the corrupted tail — this is expensive but structurally sound, and is close to what Anthropic's iterative Constitutional AI does when it routes ambiguous cases back to human raters. What any of these approaches need to know but currently don't is the counterfactual reward: what would a human actually rate these high-scoring outputs if they saw them cold, without anchoring to the comparison pairs the reward model was trained on — because preference learning from pairwise comparisons is known to be miscalibrated when the pairs are not drawn i.i.d. from the deployment distribution (see Siththaranjan et al., 2023, "Distributional Preference Learning").

The transition happens when the outputs being evaluated fall outside the range of quality variation that annotators encountered during their own implicit calibration — at that point, pairwise judgments are no longer measuring a stable underlying preference but are instead measuring something like "which of these two unfamiliar things feels less wrong," which is a different and much noisier signal. Concrete evidence: Krause et al. and subsequent replication work have shown that human pairwise preferences over generated text are not transitive at rates far above chance once output quality variance is high — meaning the Bradley-Terry model underlying most reward model training is formally misspecified, not just noisy. Anchoring specifically has been quantified in the context of LLM evaluation: Zheng et al. (2023, "Judging LLM-as-a-Judge") found position bias alone flipped preferences ~27% of the time, which means a substantial fraction of the "ground truth" labels are determined by presentation order rather than content quality. The deeper issue is that pairwise comparison is only a well-defined measurement procedure when the items being compared are in the same perceptual or quality neighborhood — psychophysics has known this since Thurstone (1927), and the just-noticeable-difference framework breaks down at large separations. So the problem becomes fundamentally one of human judgment when the policy has optimized far enough that its outputs are no longer in the same neighborhood as the comparison baseline: at that point you are asking annotators to make absolute quality judgments while forcing them into a relative judgment frame, and the resulting labels are not just noisy but systematically biased in ways that cannot be corrected by collecting more of the same kind of data.

Several better-specified alternatives exist: absolute Likert-style ratings avoid the transitivity problem but introduce calibration variance across annotators that is hard to normalize; best-worst scaling (BWS), used in some NLP annotation work, recovers more stable underlying utilities by asking annotators to pick the best and worst from a set of k items, which gives more information per judgment and implicitly anchors relative to a range rather than a single comparison. Deliberative protocols — where annotators reason explicitly before judging, or where small groups reach consensus — have been shown in moral psychology (Mercier & Sperber, 2011) and in AI-specific contexts (Irving & Askell, 2019, "AI Safety via Debate") to produce more stable and transferable judgments, but they are roughly 5-10x more expensive per label and don't parallelize the way crowdsourced pairwise comparison does. Thurstone's Case V scaling, which estimates absolute scale values from pairwise data by modeling discriminal dispersions, is statistically sounder than Bradley-Terry for heterogeneous item sets and has been used in computational linguistics (Kiritchenko & Mohammad, 2017, on sentiment intensity), yet it has essentially zero adoption in RLHF pipelines — the likely reason is that it requires enough repeated comparisons per item pair to estimate dispersions, which multiplies annotation cost by the number of items. The practical blockers are throughput and pipeline inertia: pairwise comparison via something like Mechanical Turk or a contractor workforce yields thousands of labels per hour with minimal annotator training, while any richer protocol requires domain-competent annotators, longer sessions, and quality control overhead that doesn't fit the data-flywheel model that scaled InstructGPT. The deepest blocker is that richer elicitation designs would expose a problem the current paradigm has incentive to obscure: that annotator agreement rates on the outputs of a well-optimized policy are likely far lower than the ~70-75% inter-annotator agreement rates typically reported, which are measured on early-round, lower-quality output pairs where the task is easier.

Using agreement rate as a quality gate on early-round data and then applying the trained reward model to late-round, high-variance outputs is a classic out-of-distribution generalization error dressed up as a data quality procedure — you are certifying a measuring instrument on easy cases and then deploying it on hard cases without re-certification. Concretely, if your agreement threshold is 70% and that rate is achieved on round-one SFT outputs where the quality signal is coarse and obvious, the implicit assumption is that the reward model's learned signal generalizes to round-three outputs where the quality differences are subtle and annotators would likely agree at rates closer to 55-60% — but you never measure that, so the pipeline never flags the degradation. This has a direct analogy in psychometrics: Cronbach's alpha and similar reliability estimates are sample-dependent, and a scale validated on a homogeneous population routinely shows inflated reliability that collapses when applied to a more heterogeneous one — the same instrument, the same threshold, different actual reliability. The operational implication is that the quality gate is functioning as a launch criterion for the reward model but not as a validity criterion for the regime in which it will actually be used, which means the pipeline has no internal signal that would cause it to stop or raise an alarm as overoptimization proceeds. What makes this particularly sharp is that the reward model's training loss will continue to decrease and held-out pairwise accuracy will remain high throughout later rounds — because those metrics are also computed on the same skewed, easier-than-deployment data — so every diagnostic the pipeline routinely checks will look healthy precisely when the underlying calibration is failing.

The most reliable external signal is a divergence between the reward model's score distribution and an independent human evaluation on the same outputs sampled from the current policy — if RM scores are climbing across rounds while blind human ratings on those outputs plateau or decline, that gap is the overoptimization signature, and it requires no access to the RM's internals. Gao et al. (2022) operationalized almost exactly this by maintaining a "gold" reward model (a larger, separately trained proxy for human judgment) and tracking its scores against the optimized RM's scores as KL increased — the divergence between gold and proxy RM scores as a function of KL budget is perhaps the cleanest published early-warning curve, showing detectable separation well before the policy produces outputs that are obviously degraded to casual inspection. A second external signal is output diversity collapse: an overoptimizing policy concentrates on reward-model-exploiting modes, which shows up as a measurable drop in n-gram or embedding-space diversity of generated outputs even when individual outputs still look fluent — this is detectable with no human labels at all, just distributional statistics on policy samples across rounds. A third, more subtle signal is evaluator disagreement asymmetry: as outputs move into overoptimized territory, human raters don't just disagree more — they disagree in a structured way where one rater finds the output impressive and another finds it subtly off, which produces a bimodal rating distribution rather than a unimodal noisy one; that bimodality is detectable with small samples (~50-100 outputs) if you collect per-rater scores rather than adjudicated labels. The practical obstacle is that all three signals require either a held-out gold evaluator, ongoing human sampling, or distributional monitoring infrastructure that sits outside the core training loop — and current pipelines are typically optimized for throughput, meaning the monitoring apparatus is the first thing that gets cut when annotation budgets are constrained.
